claim: Cortico-striatal projections are an essential part of the brain's attention–motor interface.
source: Cortico-striatal projections are an essential part of the brain's attention–motor interface.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about brain function.

claim: GTs executed more cued turns than STs.
source: GTs executed more cued turns and initiated such turns more slowly than STs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: GTs initiated cued turns more slowly than STs.
source: GTs executed more cued turns and initiated such turns more slowly than STs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: During turns, cue-evoked glutamate concentrations were higher in GTs than in STs.
source: During turns, but not missed turns or cued stops, cue-evoked glutamate concentrations were higher in GTs than in STs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: During missed turns, cue-evoked glutamate concentrations were not higher in GTs than in STs.
source: During turns, but not missed turns or cued stops, cue-evoked glutamate concentrations were higher in GTs than in STs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: During cued stops, cue-evoked glutamate concentrations were not higher in GTs than in STs.
source: During turns, but not missed turns or cued stops, cue-evoked glutamate concentrations were higher in GTs than in STs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: In STs, turn cue-locked glutamate concentrations frequently peaked twice or three times.
source: In STs, turn cue-locked glutamate concentrations frequently peaked twice or three times, contrasting with predominately single peaks in GTs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In GTs, turn cue-locked glutamate concentrations predominantly showed single peaks.
source: In STs, turn cue-locked glutamate concentrations frequently peaked twice or three times, contrasting with predominately single peaks in GTs.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In GTs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated turn rates.
source: In GTs, but not STs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated turn rates and turn cue-evoked glutamate concentrations and increased the number of turn cue-locked glutamate peaks.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: In GTs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated turn cue-evoked glutamate concentrations.
source: In GTs, but not STs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated turn rates and turn cue-evoked glutamate concentrations and increased the number of turn cue-locked glutamate peaks.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8g.

claim: In GTs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections increased the number of turn cue-locked glutamate peaks.
source: In GTs, but not STs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated turn rates and turn cue-evoked glutamate concentrations and increased the number of turn cue-locked glutamate peaks.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8h.

claim: In STs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections did not attenuate turn rates.
source: In GTs, but not STs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated turn rates and turn cue-evoked glutamate concentrations and increased the number of turn cue-locked glutamate peaks.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: Turn cue-evoked glutamate release in GTs is tightly controlled by cortico-striatal neuronal activity.
source: These findings indicate that turn cue-evoked glutamate release in GTs is tightly controlled by cortico-striatal neuronal activity.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and is based on the experimental findings regarding DREADD inhibition effects.

claim: In STs, glutamate release from DMS glutamatergic terminals may be regulated by other striatal circuitry.
source: In contrast, in STs, glutamate release from DMS glutamatergic terminals may be regulated by other striatal circuitry, preferably mediating cued suppression of action and reward tracking.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation in the abstract based on the differential effects of DREADD inhibition.

claim: Cortico-striatal dysfunction has been hypothesized to contribute to complex movement control deficits in Parkinson's disease.
source: As cortico-striatal dysfunction has been hypothesized to contribute to a wide range of disorders, including complex movement control deficits in Parkinson's disease and compulsive drug taking, the demonstration of phenotypic contrasts in cortico-striatal control implies the presence of individual vulnerabilities for such disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior hypotheses in the literature.

claim: Cortico-striatal dysfunction has been hypothesized to contribute to compulsive drug taking.
source: As cortico-striatal dysfunction has been hypothesized to contribute to a wide range of disorders, including complex movement control deficits in Parkinson's disease and compulsive drug taking, the demonstration of phenotypic contrasts in cortico-striatal control implies the presence of individual vulnerabilities for such disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior hypotheses in the literature.

claim: Phenotypic contrasts in cortico-striatal control imply the presence of individual vulnerabilities for neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: As cortico-striatal dysfunction has been hypothesized to contribute to a wide range of disorders, including complex movement control deficits in Parkinson's disease and compulsive drug taking, the demonstration of phenotypic contrasts in cortico-striatal control implies the presence of individual vulnerabilities for such disorders.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Fronto-striatal projections play an essential role in the integration of information about attended cues into striatal circuitry.
source: Fronto-striatal projections have been thought to play an essential role in the integration of information about attended cues into striatal circuitry, to prioritize cue-linked action and facilitate modification of action selection in response to changing action outcomes (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; van Schouwenburg et al., 2012; Chatham et al., 2014; Hart et al., 2018a; Hart et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Deficient or biased cortico-striatal functions has been postulated to cause neuropsychiatric symptoms ranging from complex movement control deficits in Parkinson's disease to compulsive addictive drug use.
source: Deficient or biased cortico-striatal functions has been postulated to cause neuropsychiatric symptoms ranging from complex movement control deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD) to compulsive addictive drug use (Volkow et al., 2006; Bohnen et al., 2009; Ersche et al., 2011; Marshall and Ostlund, 2018; Rasooli et al., 2021; Sarter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Prelimbic projections to dorsomedial striatum were previously demonstrated to be necessary for learning goal-directed actions.
source: Focusing on the prelimbic projections to dorsomedial striatum (DMS) (Mailly et al., 2013), that previously were demonstrated to be necessary for learning goal-directed actions (Hart et al., 2018b; Choi et al., 2023), we measured real-time, cue- and reward-locked glutamate concentrations in the DMS using amperometry and glutamate-sensing electrodes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: People with PD who experience a propensity for falls exhibit deficient turns.
source: The development of this Cued-Triggered Turning Task (CTTT; Avila et al., 2020) was inspired by evidence showing that people with PD who experience a propensity for falls exhibit deficient turns (Stack and Ashburn, 2008; Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In people with PD, an elevated risk for falls has been attributed to loss of cholinergic neurons innervating cortical regions.
source: In people with PD, such an elevated risk for falls has been attributed to loss of cholinergic neurons innervating cortical regions and the resulting failure to attend to, and thus select and evaluate, movement cues (Bohnen et al., 2009; Yarnall et al., 2011; Rochester et al., 2012; Bohnen et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Rats with combined cortical cholinergic and striatal dopaminergic losses and a propensity for falls exhibit deficits in cued turning, but not cued stopping.
source: We previously demonstrated the usefulness of the CTTT for modeling clinically relevant, attentional-motor deficiencies by showing that rats with combined cortical cholinergic and striatal dopaminergic losses and a propensity for falls (Kucinski et al., 2013; Kucinski et al., 2019; Kucinski and Sarter, 2021; Sarter et al., 2021) exhibit deficits in cued turning, but not cued stopping (Avila et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Goal-trackers orient to a Pavlovian reward cue and learn its predictive significance, but do not approach and contact such a cue.
source: Goal-trackers (GTs) orient to a Pavlovian reward cue, that is, they learn its predictive significance, but they do not approach and contact such a cue.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a defining characteristic of GTs.

claim: Sign-trackers approach and contact a Pavlovian cue, which has been interpreted as assigning incentive salience to the cue.
source: In contrast, sign-trackers (STs) approach and contact such a cue, which has been interpreted as assigning incentive salience to a Pavlovian cue and attributed to cue-evoked mesolimbic dopamine signaling (Flagel et al., 2011; Flagel and Robinson, 2017; Iglesias et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The relatively greater vulnerability of STs for addictive drug taking and relapse in the presence of Pavlovian drug cues has been extensively documented.
source: The relatively greater vulnerability of STs for addictive drug taking and relapse in the presence of Pavlovian drug cues has been extensively documented (e.g., Saunders and Robinson, 2010; Yager and Robinson, 2010; Yager and Robinson, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Goal- and sign-tracking index the presence of broader, opponent cognitive-motivational styles dominated by a bias toward deploying top–down and bottom–up processing of action cues, respectively.
source: Goal- and sign-tracking index the presence of broader, opponent cognitive-motivational styles that are dominated by a bias toward deploying top–down (or goal-directed) and bottom–up (or stimulus-driven) processing of action cues, respectively (for review see Sarter and Phillips, 2018; for evidence of the presence of these traits in humans see Schad et al., 2020; Colaizzi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Biases of GTs and STs were previously shown to be mediated in part via contrasting cholinergic capacities for the detection of cues.
source: As such biases of GTs and STs were previously shown to be mediated in part via contrasting cholinergic capacities for the detection of cues (Paolone et al., 2013; Koshy Cherian et al., 2017; Pitchers et al., 2017a; Pitchers et al., 2017b), we hypothesized that contrasts in the cortico-striatal processing of movement cues contribute to the expression of these opponent biases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PCA screening of N = 378 (215 females) rats yielded 113 GTs (30%), 155 rats with intermediate scores (INs; 41%), and 110 STs (29%).
source: PCA screening of N = 378 (215 females) rats yielded 113 GTs (30%), 155 rats with intermediate scores (INs; 41%), and 110 STs (29%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the phenotype screening outcomes.

claim: The distribution of PCA scores did not differ by sex.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Pitchers et al., 2015), the distribution of PCA scores did not differ by sex (X2(2, N = 378) = 0.35, p = 0.56; Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The distribution of PCA scores from rats obtained from the two vendors differed significantly.
source: However, the distribution of PCA scores from rats obtained from the two vendors differed significantly (X2(2, N = 378) = 36.62, p < 0.001; Figure 1c; note that the percentages of phenotypes shown in Figure 1c were calculated individually for each vendor).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Relatively more rats obtained from Inotiv displayed lever-directed behaviors, while rats supplied by Taconic relatively more frequently exhibited goal cup-directed behaviors.
source: Relatively more rats obtained from Inotiv displayed lever-directed behaviors, while rats supplied by Taconic relatively more frequently exhibited goal cup-directed behaviors (see also Fitzpatrick et al., 2013; Gileta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The number of training sessions required by GTs and STs to reach CTTT criterion performance did not differ significantly.
source: The number of training sessions required by GTs (n = 29, 13 females) and STs (n = 22, 12 females; Figure 2) to reach CTTT criterion performance, defined as 70% correct responses to either cue for two consecutive sessions, did not differ significantly (F(1,47) = 0.01, p = 0.94; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 4a.

claim: After having reached performance criterion, GTs scored significantly more cued turns than STs across four subsequent test sessions.
source: After having reached performance criterion, GTs scored significantly more cued turns than STs across four subsequent test sessions (main effect of phenotype: F(1,47) = 5.03, p = 0.003, ηp2 = 0.097; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 4b.

claim: The proportion of cued stops following stop cue presentation did not differ by phenotype, day, or sex.
source: The proportion of cued stops following stop cue presentation did not differ by phenotype, day, or sex (all main effects and interactions: all F < 3.06; all p > 0.052; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 4d.

claim: Relative to the time of cue onset, GTs initiated and completed cued turns significantly later than STs.
source: Relative to the time of cue onset, GTs initiated and completed cued turns significantly later than STs (main effects of phenotype; initiation: F(1,51) = 8.84, p = 0.005, ηp2 = 0.16; completion: F(1,51) = 9.40, p = 0.004, ηp2 = 0.17; Figure 4e; effects of sex and interactions between the effects of sex and phenotype: all F < 1.03, all p > 0.32).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 4e.

claim: The time needed to complete turns did not differ between the phenotypes.
source: Reflecting the parallel effects of phenotype on initiation and completion time relative to cue onset, the time needed to complete turns, that is, the time from turn initiation to completion, did not differ between the phenotypes (main effects of phenotype, sex, and interactions: all F < 3.51, all p > 0.07; GTs: 2.7 ± 0.2 s (M, SEM); STs: 2.3 ± 0.2 s).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Maximum glutamate peak concentrations recorded during the cue period, and followed by turns, were significantly higher in GTs than in STs.
source: Maximum glutamate peak concentrations recorded during the cue period, and followed by turns, were significantly higher in GTs than in STs phenotype: F(1,28.85) = 8.85, p = 0.006, ηp2 = 0.23 (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 6c.

claim: The presence of single peaks predominantly characterized cue-locked recordings from GTs while two or three peaks occurred relatively more frequently in STs.
source: Furthermore, the presence of single peaks predominantly characterized cue-locked recordings from GTs while two or three peaks occurred relatively more frequently in STs (X2(2, N = 192) = 1 6.36, p = 0.0003; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 6d.

claim: Recordings during cue periods that were followed by failures to turn indicated higher maximum peak amplitudes in STs when compared to GTs.
source: Recordings during cue periods that were followed by failures to turn, or misses, indicated higher maximum peak amplitudes in STs when compared to GTs (missed turns: F(1,193) = 55.20, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.22, Figure 6e; no phenotype effects on peak number; not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 6e.

claim: Relatively higher maximum peak amplitudes in STs were recorded during stop cue periods when followed by stops.
source: Likewise, relatively higher maximum peak amplitudes in STs were recorded during stop cue periods when followed by stops (F(1,27.67) = 33.32, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55, Figure 6f)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 6f.

claim: Relatively higher maximum peak amplitudes in STs were recorded locked to reward delivery.
source: Likewise, relatively higher maximum peak amplitudes in STs were recorded during stop cue periods when followed by stops (F(1,27.67) = 33.32, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55, Figure 6f) and locked to reward delivery (F(1,19.28) = 28.88, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.40, Figure 6g; note that errors in response to stop cues – false turns – were rare and therefore not analyzed).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 6g.

claim: Turn cue-evoked glutamate maximum peak concentrations greater than 2.8 µM were followed by disproportionally more turns in GTs than STs.
source: Turn cue-evoked glutamate maximum peak concentrations greater than 2.8 µM were followed by disproportionally more turns in GTs than STs (2.8–8 µM: p = 0.045 to <0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: With increasing glutamate maximum threshold concentrations, GTs were 1.12 (>2.8 µM) to 1.40 (>8 µM) times as likely as STs to turn.
source: With increasing glutamate maximum threshold concentrations, GTs were 1.12 (>2.8 µM) to 1.40 (>8 µM) times as likely as STs to turn (middle curve, circles in Figure 7a; concentrations >10 µM yielded contingency table cell counts of n < 10 and thus were not included).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 7a.

claim: If one single glutamate peak occurred following the onset of turn cues, GTs were 1.43 times as likely as STs to turn.
source: Furthermore, if one single glutamate peak occurred following the onset of turn cues and during the 2-s cue presentation period, GTs were 1.43 times as likely as STs to turn (p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Following two and three glutamate peaks, GTs were only 0.74 times as likely as STs to turn.
source: In contrast to the significantly higher odds for turns in GTs following a single cue-evoked glutamate peak, following two and three glutamate peaks (no more than three turn cue-locked peaks were observed), GTs were only 0.74 times as likely as STs to turn (p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Administration of CNO reduced the ratio of turns/turn cue trials in GTs by nearly 50%.
source: The effects of phenotype and treatment interacted significantly (F(1,20) = 35.99, p < 0.0001, ηp² = 0.64) reflecting that CNO reduced the ratio of turns/turn cue trials in GTs by nearly 50% (for multiple comparisons see Figure 8e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 8e.

claim: Turn rates in STs were unaffected by CNO.
source: The effects of phenotype and treatment interacted significantly (F(1,20) = 35.99, p < 0.0001, ηp² = 0.64) reflecting that CNO reduced the ratio of turns/turn cue trials in GTs by nearly 50% (for multiple comparisons see Figure 8e). This analysis also indicated a main effect of phenotype (F(1,20) = 9.45, p = 0.006) that likewise reflected the greatly suppressed turn rates in GTs treated with CNO while turn rates in STs were unaffected by CNO (M, SEM: GTs: 0.54 ± 0.04 turns/turn cue trials; STs: 0.71 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: In GTs expressing the empty control vector, CNO did not affect the relative number of cued turns.
source: To control for potential off-target effects of CNO, the effects of CNO (5.0 mg/kg) and vehicle on the relative number of cued turns were assessed in GTs expressing the empty control vector (n = 5). In these rats, CNO did not affect the relative number of cued turns (t(3) = 0.78, p = 0.50; means: vehicle: 0.77 turns/turn cue trials; CNO: 0.73).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Administration of CNO significantly reduced turn cue-locked maximum peak glutamate concentrations in GTs, but not STs.
source: Administration of CNO significantly reduced turn cue-locked maximum peak glutamate concentrations in GTs, but not STs phenotype × treatment (F(1,200.79) = 18.42, p < 0.001; main effect of treatment: F(1,200.79) = 44.76, p < 0.001; phenotype: F(1,9.50) = 0.73, p = 0.41).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Administration of CNO in GTs reduced the number of single peak and increased the number of two-peak occurrences.
source: Administration of CNO in GTs reduced the number of single peak and increased the number of two-peak occurrences but, in STs, did not affect the frequencies of one, two, or three peak occurrences (separate Chi-squared tests on the effects of vehicle and CNO on frequencies; GTs: X2(2, N = 99) = 17.87, p < 0.001; STs: X2(2, N = 107) = 0.03, p = 0.98; Figure 8h).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 8h.

claim: Administration of CNO significantly increased the time GTs took to initiate turns, relative to cue onset, when compared with vehicle-treated GTs and CNO-treated STs.
source: Administration of CNO significantly increased the time GTs took to initiate turns, relative to cue onset, when compared with vehicle-treated GTs and CNO-treated STs (LMM; phenotype × treatment: F(1,173.72) = 9.70, p = 0.002, ηp2 = 0.05; see Figure 8i for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 8i.

claim: When followed by misses, CNO had no effect on turn cue-locked maximum glutamate concentrations in GTs.
source: In contrast to turn cue-locked maximum glutamate concentrations in trials followed by turns, when followed by misses, CNO had no effect (main effect of treatment: F(1,133.99) = 1.62, p = 0.21; Figure 8j).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 8j.

claim: CNO significantly reduced cue-locked maximum peak concentrations in STs in trials yielding misses.
source: However, a significant interaction between the effects of treatment and phenotype (F(1,133.99) = 3.88, p = 0.04; ηp2 = 0.03) reflected that CNO significantly reduced cue-locked maximum peak concentrations in STs in trials yielding misses (results of multiple comparisons are shown in Figure 8j).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 8j.

claim: There were no effects of CNO on stop cue-locked maximum peak glutamate concentrations.
source: There were no effects of CNO on stop cue-locked maximum peak glutamate concentrations, irrespective of whether the stop cue was followed by a stop or a (false) turn (all p > 0.23; not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Peak glutamate concentrations locked to reward delivery were higher in STs than in GTs.
source: As before (Figure 6g), peak glutamate concentrations locked to reward delivery were higher in STs than in GTs (main effect of phenotype: F(1,10.45) = 22.38, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.68; Figure 8k).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 8k.

claim: CNO administration resulted in a significant decrease of reward-locked glutamate maximum peak concentrations in both phenotypes.
source: CNO administration resulted in a significant decrease of reward-locked glutamate maximum peak concentrations in both phenotypes (main effect of treatment: F(1,412.73) = 4.83, p = 0.03, ηp2 = 0.01; interaction: F(1,412.729) = 1.35, p = 0.25; Figure 8k).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 8k.

claim: In GTs, but not STs, the expression efficacy of mCherry in the prelimbic cortex was significantly correlated with the efficacy of CNO to attenuate cued turns.
source: In contrast, in GTs, but not STs, the expression efficacy of mCherry in the prelimbic cortex, that is, of the inhibitory DREADD construct, was significantly correlated with the efficacy of CNO to attenuate cued turns (GTs: R2 = 0.48, p = 0.02; STs: R2 = 0.06, p = 0.51; Figure 9g).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 9g.

claim: In GTs, but not STs, the proportion of neurons expressing both the reporter for the inhibitory DREADD and the retrogradely transported Cre-expressing construct was positively correlated with CNO-induced reduction of cued turns.
source: Likewise, in GTs, but not STs, the proportion of neurons expressing both the reporter for the inhibitory DREADD and the retrogradely transported Cre-expressing construct was positively correlated with CNO-induced reduction of cued turns (GTs: R2 = 0.77, p = 0.0004; STs: R2 = 0.06, p = 0.51; Figure 9j).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to Figure 9j.

claim: In GTs, the degree of CNO-induced inhibition of prelimbic cortex–DMS projections predicted the efficacy of CNO to attenuate cued turning rates.
source: Thus, in GTs, the degree of CNO-induced inhibition of prelimbic cortex–DMS projections predicted the efficacy of CNO to attenuate cued turning rates.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on the correlation analyses.

claim: In GTs, turn cue processing in the striatum is closely controlled by cortico-striatal activity.
source: The present findings indicate that, in GTs, turn cue processing in the striatum of is closely controlled by cortico-striatal activity, and that they utilize turn cues more reliably than STs.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: GTs utilize turn cues more reliably than STs.
source: The present findings indicate that, in GTs, turn cue processing in the striatum of is closely controlled by cortico-striatal activity, and that they utilize turn cues more reliably than STs.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: GTs out-performed STs in tasks taxing the attentional detection of cues, in part by deploying goal-directed attentional mechanisms to detect cues and maintain stable task performance.
source: GTs out-performed STs in tasks taxing the attentional detection of cues, in part by deploying goal-directed attentional mechanisms to detect cues and maintain stable task performance (e.g., Paolone et al., 2013; Kucinski et al., 2018; Phillips and Sarter, 2020; Kucinski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In GTs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated cued turns and associated glutamate concentrations.
source: In GTs, inhibition of prelimbic–DMS projections attenuated cued turns and associated glutamate concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing the experimental findings.

claim: Suppression of movement during cued stops and associated glutamate release dynamics remained unaffected by CNO.
source: In contrast, suppression of movement, as seen during cued stops, and associated glutamate release dynamics, remained unaffected by CNO and, therefore, may not depend on cortico-striatal processing of movement cues (see also Vandaele et al., 2019; Cruz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Cued stops may not depend on cortico-striatal processing of movement cues.
source: In contrast, suppression of movement, as seen during cued stops, and associated glutamate release dynamics, remained unaffected by CNO and, therefore, may not depend on cortico-striatal processing of movement cues (see also Vandaele et al., 2019; Cruz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the experimental findings with supporting citations.

claim: In GTs, turn cue-evoked glutamate concentrations may depend on the cue detection-mediating generation of single cholinergic transients in prelimbic cortex.
source: In GTs, turn cue-evoked glutamate concentrations as well as the presence of single peaks may be speculated to depend, or be secondary to, the cue detection-mediating generation of single cholinergic transients in prelimbic cortex and the resulting generation of high-frequency oscillations (Gritton et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2017; see also Introduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation with supporting citations.

claim: In the DMS, single high-amplitude glutamate transients from cortical afferents may recruit multiple populations of interneurons and striatal output neurons, thereby forming fronto-striatal cell assemblies to force cue-associated action selection.
source: In the DMS, single high-amplitude glutamate transients from cortical afferents may recruit multiple populations of interneurons and striatal output neurons, thereby forming, for a precise period of time, fronto-striatal cell assemblies to force cue-associated action selection (see also Hart et al., 2018a; Hart et al., 2018b; Oberto et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation with supporting citations.

claim: Cortico-striatal glutamatergic terminals are recruited, directly and indirectly, via striatal interneurons and striatal dopaminergic afferents, thereby supporting bidirectional glutamatergic–dopaminergic interactions.
source: Cortico-striatal glutamatergic terminals are also recruited, directly and indirectly, via striatal interneurons and striatal dopaminergic afferents, thereby supporting bidirectional glutamatergic–dopaminergic interactions and allowing reward expectation and action outcome to influence the glutamatergic representation of movement cues (Bamford et al., 2004; Agnoli et al., 2013; Kosillo et al., 2016; Cai and Ford, 2018; Moss et al., 2021; Chantranupong et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2023; Krok et al., 2023; Holly et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Striatal control of cortico-striatal terminals may preferentially yield suppression of action in STs.
source: Such striatal control of cortico-striatal terminals, primarily via cholinergic and dopaminergic heteroreceptors (for review see Lovinger et al., 2022), may preferentially yield suppression of action in STs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation with supporting citations.

claim: In STs, glutamatergic transients may primarily signal the expectation of reward and the heightened perceptual value of a reward predicting cue.
source: Thus, in STs, glutamatergic transients may be speculated to primarily signal the expectation of reward, and also the heightened perceptual value of a reward predicting cue (see also Pitchers et al., 2017a; Saunders et al., 2018; Iglesias et al., 2023; Bernklau et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation with supporting citations.

claim: The findings predict a greater vulnerability of PD patients who preferentially utilize cortico-striatal mechanisms to process movement cues for cholinergic loss-associated impairments in cued movement control and for the propensity for falls.
source: Consistent with the view that striatal pathology contributes little to the explanation of individual, clinical severity of PD (Johansson et al., 2024), our findings predict a greater vulnerability of PD patients who preferentially utilize cortico-striatal mechanisms to process movement cues, that is, GTs, for cholinergic loss-associated impairments in cued movement control and for the propensity for falls (Sarter et al., 2014; Sarter et al., 2021; Albin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a prediction based on the experimental findings with supporting citations.

claim: STs may generally be less efficient in executing cued movements, particularly in situations featuring complex and competing movement cues.
source: In contrast, STs may generally be less efficient in executing cued movements, particularly in situations featuring complex and competing movement cues (e.g., Beaulne-Séguin and Nantel, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation with supporting citations.

claim: All rats orient toward the CS, that is, all rats learn the predictive significance of the CS.
source: Prior analyses have consistently shown that all rats orient toward the CS, that is, all rats learn the predictive significance of the CS, but only some – the STs – approach and contact the CS (Figure 1a, top right photo), while GTs do not contact the CS but approach and enter the food port (Figure 1a, bottom right photo; e.g., Robinson and Flagel, 2009; Meyer et al., 2012; Pitchers et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Only some rats – the STs – approach and contact the CS.
source: Prior analyses have consistently shown that all rats orient toward the CS, that is, all rats learn the predictive significance of the CS, but only some – the STs – approach and contact the CS (Figure 1a, top right photo), while GTs do not contact the CS but approach and enter the food port (Figure 1a, bottom right photo; e.g., Robinson and Flagel, 2009; Meyer et al., 2012; Pitchers et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: GTs do not contact the CS but approach and enter the food port.
source: Prior analyses have consistently shown that all rats orient toward the CS, that is, all rats learn the predictive significance of the CS, but only some – the STs – approach and contact the CS (Figure 1a, top right photo), while GTs do not contact the CS but approach and enter the food port (Figure 1a, bottom right photo; e.g., Robinson and Flagel, 2009; Meyer et al., 2012; Pitchers et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Glutamate peaks reflect the orchestrated yet asynchronous depolarization of glutamatergic terminals over several hundreds of milliseconds and within fractions of micrometers from the electrode surface.
source: Our analyses of glutamate peak characteristics were guided by the view that such peaks reflect the orchestrated yet asynchronous depolarization of glutamatergic terminals, over several hundreds of milliseconds and within fractions of micrometers from the electrode surface, and likely sufficient to stimulate synaptic and extra-synaptic, relatively low-affinity glutamate receptors (Hascup et al., 2008; Parikh et al., 2008; Parikh et al., 2010; Mattinson et al., 2011; Quintero et al., 2011; Parikh et al., 2014) (e.g., Clements et al., 1992; Rusakov and Kullmann, 1998; Budisantoso et al., 2013; Matthews et al., 2022; Mendonça et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Implanted MEAs maintain stable sensitivity and reliability for at least 7 days after implantation.
source: Consistent with prior evidence showing that implanted MEAs maintain stable sensitivity and reliability for at least 7 days after implantation, electrochemical recordings were completed within 7 days of MEA implantation (Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citations.

claim: Peak concentrations of extracellular glutamate indicate the degree and extent of terminal depolarization.
source: Prior studies on the effects of depolarization of synaptic terminals, blocking such depolarization, or of pharmacological manipulations of the excitability of terminals, confirmed that peak concentrations of extracellular glutamate indicate the degree and extent of terminal depolarization (Hascup et al., 2008; Parikh et al., 2008; Parikh et al., 2010; Mattinson et al., 2011; Quintero et al., 2011; Parikh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citations.

claim: The CTTT required rats to walk on a treadmill at a walking speed of 9.6 cm/s.
source: The CTTT required rats to walk on a treadmill (walking speed: 9.6 cm/s).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3 caption describing the task parameters.

claim: Presentation of a turn or stop cue for 2 s indicated that the treadmill stopped 1 s later.
source: Presentation of a turn or stop cue for 2 s indicated that the treadmill stopped 1 s later, and restarted after a 5-s pause, in the reverse or same direction, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3 caption describing the task parameters.

claim: The treadmill restarted after a 5-s pause in the reverse or same direction for turn or stop cues, respectively.
source: Presentation of a turn or stop cue for 2 s indicated that the treadmill stopped 1 s later, and restarted after a 5-s pause, in the reverse or same direction, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3 caption describing the task parameters.

claim: Successful turns and stops were rewarded by delivering a 45 mg banana pellet on average 3.6 s following cue offset.
source: Successful turns and stops without turns, respectively, were rewarded by delivering a 45 mg banana pellet, on average 3.6 s following cue offset (see green square in d).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3 caption describing the task parameters.

claim: Successive presentation of cues was separated by a variable intertrial interval (ITI) of 60 ± 45 s.
source: Successive presentation of cues was separated by a variable intertrial interval (ITI) of 60 ± 45 s during which the rat continued walking the treadmill.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3 caption describing the task parameters.
